description: This team is for students at City College of San Francisco looking to challenge themselves
summary: Our project is an easy to use app that shows users statistics involving the conditions of a south pole site, allowing the user to determine whether said site is a good candidate for landing. The app also allows the user to look into a future time frame, to determine whether setting up at the site is plausible due to its conditions. The project is important because NASA already has tools, but they're complicated, making it difficult to evaluate critical information. Our app cuts the complication, making it easy for the users to simply change the time period and site to gather the important information. The target audience of the app is mainly for educators and students, which is why we included a 3D model of the terrain since they might not know how the terrain would look.
details: To answer the challenge of creating an intuitive tool that helps mission planners, educators, and the public determine candidate landing sites and compare landing sites, we created an app that shows important statistics, graphs, and what a 3D model of the terrain would look like. The important statistics include the % sunlit in a time frame, % earth visibility, % of both at the same time, the longest streak without sunlight, and power production of a solar panel. The statistics were determined with public data of real terrain from LOLA elevation models (DEMs) and spherical astronomy. The app also allows users to change panel metrics to determine average power and energy per day. The app is easy to use and allows users who don't know how to use public complicated NASA calculators what conditions would look like at the south pole. The app also allows users to look at conditions in the future, which could allow users to determine whether the site is a good candidate for landing. Though, the statistics only factor in the small part of the map, only limited to the dimensions of the provided topography elevation models (far away terrain wasn't included in the calculations). We used majority python to code the calculators, and used python libraries to get access to functions not built into python (rasterio, skyfield, streamlit, plotly, pandas, pyarrow, numpy tifffile). What our team factored in was displaying solar panel metrics and a 3D model of the topography of certain terrain maps.
dataRefs: High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites
